detail.longDescription: On 10 November, a PHP package released version 5.2.0. According to its own date field, it was three years old. Harmless this time. The release tag pointed at a 2022 commit. But that date field belongs to the package author, and it can be backdated. A waiting period based on it would have treated a brand-new release as ancient. PHP's package manager, Composer, got a cooldown in version 2.11. It counts from the moment the registry first saw a release, a timestamp the registry sets itself. The Composer team recommends a few hours to a day. We took the full day, on purpose. Our automated updates get committed and released without a human looking at them. The cooldown detects nothing. It buys time for somebody to notice a bad release before our pipeline installs it. Longer hurts, though. With one week in my lab, an update got stuck: the fixes for a known vulnerability were still waiting, and the older versions were blocked as vulnerable. Too young or too dangerous, pick one. The hard question is security fixes. Should they skip the wait? The Composer team says no, deliberately: an attacker with access to a package's repository can publish an advisory, too. Fair point. Our sites run on Drupal, though, and its Security Team publishes the advisories, not the package maintainer. So fixes for those advisories may skip the wait. Only releases published before the advisory was reported. Anything published later waits the full day. That exception is our call, not Composer's. The full write-up, including a spell checker that reordered my rollout: https://go.lakedrops.com/composer-cooldown Who would you trust to say "this one can't wait"? I write these myself. AI is a tool in my harness: it doesn't think and it doesn't write, it makes me write better. Every claim is mine and checked by me. # SupplyChainSecurity # OpenSource # DevOps # PHP
